tip: σχολή (scholi) is a university department – σχολείο (scholio) is the kids' school. Same root, easy to mix up.
Greek has a verb for being late: άργησα να στείλω (argisa na stilo) = I was late to send. No adjective needed – the verb carries the whole 'was late'.
Greek holds notes where English takes them: κρατάω σημειώσεις (kratao simiosis) = literally 'I hold notes'.
ιδιαίτερα (idietera) usually means 'especially' – but κάνω ιδιαίτερα (kano idietera) = I give private lessons. Context decides which.
Masculine nouns in -ές take a -δες plural: ο καφές → καφέδες (kafes → kafedes) = coffees. Not the simple -ς swap you'd expect.
βάση (vasi) means 'base' – in the exam system it's the admission cutoff: πέρασα τη βάση (perasa ti vasi) = I made the cutoff.
αντιγράφω (andigrafo) means 'copy' – and it is also the word for cheating on a test. αντιγραφή (andigrafi) = the cheating itself.
Doubling the negative is correct Greek: δεν κατάλαβα τίποτα (den katalava tipota) = literally 'I didn't understand nothing'. δεν and τίποτα always pair up.
παρέα (parea) means 'company, friend group' – after a verb it means 'together': μελετάμε παρέα (meletame parea) = we study as a group.
όρεξη (orexi) is literally 'appetite' – Greek stretches it to any desire: δεν έχω όρεξη (den echo orexi) = I don't feel like it.
κολλάει (kolaei) is literally 'it sticks' – a buffering video sticks in Greek. The same verb covers frozen apps and being stuck in traffic.
κινητό (kinito) is literally 'the movable one' – the everyday word for a mobile phone. τηλέφωνο (tilefono) sounds more formal.
The απο- (apo-) prefix undoes a verb: συνδέομαι (sindeome) = log in, αποσυνδέομαι (aposindeome) = log out. It works like English dis- or un-.
ανεβάζω/κατεβάζω (anevazo/katevazo) are literally 'take up'/'take down' = upload/download: ανέβασα μια φωτογραφία (anevasa mia fotografia) = I posted a photo.
μου τελείωσαν τα δεδομένα (mou teliosan ta dedomena) = literally 'the data ran out on me'. The data is the subject – you're just the affected μου (mou).
κλείνω (klino) means 'close' – and it's the booking verb: έκλεισα εισιτήρια (eklisa isitiria) = I booked tickets. Tables and rooms get 'closed' too.
You answer TO a call in Greek: απάντησα στην κλήση (apandisa stin klisi). απαντάω (apandao) always takes σε (se) before the thing answered.
πιο (pio) before an adjective means 'more' – no ending change. Add the article and it becomes 'most': ο πιο στενός (o pio stenos) = the closest.
κάναμε παρέα (kaname parea) is literally 'we made company' = we hung out. κάνω παρέα με (kano parea me) is the everyday way to say you hang out with someone.
λείπω (lipo) flips English 'miss': the missed person is the subject. λείπεις στην παρέα (lipis stin parea) = 'you are missing to the group' – the group misses you.
γνωρίζω (gnorizo) means 'know' – its past means 'met': τη γνώρισα (ti gnorisa) = I met her, got to know her for the first time.
στηρίζουμε ο ένας τον άλλον (stirizoume o enas ton alon) = we support one another – literally 'the one the other', the fixed reciprocal formula.
της (tis) before the verb = 'to her': της εμπιστεύομαι (tis embistevome) = I entrust to her. Greek trusts things TO people, and the pronoun comes first.
κρατάω (kratao) means 'hold' – with a time span it means 'last': η φιλία μας κρατάει είκοσι χρόνια (i filia mas kratai ikosi chronia) = our friendship has lasted twenty years.
από παιδιά (apo pedia) is literally 'from kids' = since childhood: φίλοι από παιδιά (fili apo pedia) = friends since we were kids.
χαίρομαι (cherome) ends in -ομαι and looks passive, but it simply means 'I'm glad'. Many feeling verbs exist only in this -ομαι shape.
περνάμε ωραία (pername orea) is literally 'we pass nicely' = we have a good time. In Greek you pass time well, you don't have it.
σαν (san) = 'like' for resemblance: σαν αδερφή (san aderfi) = like a sister. For matching how something is done, Greek switches to όπως (opos).
μου αρέσει (mou aresi) works backwards: the liked person is the subject – literally 'he pleases me'. That's why the verb isn't first person.
εδώ και δύο χρόνια (edo ke dio chronia) = 'for two years now'. εδώ και + a time span, with the present tense, covers English 'have been ... for'.
παντρεύονται (pandrevonde) looks passive but means plain 'they marry'. Some verbs exist only in the -ομαι family – marrying is one of them.
Object pronouns go before the verb: μας σύστησαν (mas sistisan) = literally 'us they-introduced'. Short pronouns always sit ahead in Greek.
μεταξύ τους (metaxi tous) is literally 'between them' – Greek for 'each other': μοιάζουν πολύ μεταξύ τους (miazoun poli metaxi tous) = they look a lot alike.
μοιάζω σε (miazo se) = resemble TO someone: μοιάζει στον παππού (miazi ston pappou) = takes after her grandfather. The σε is required – no direct object.
δεν αντέχω (den andecho) = I can't bear it – stronger than δεν μπορώ (den boro), the plain 'I can't'. αντέχω is about endurance running out.
δεμένη (demeni) is literally 'tied': δεμένη οικογένεια (demeni ikogenia) = close-knit family. Greek ties families together where English knits them.
The τα (ta) in τα πάει καλά (ta pai kala) = 'gets along' points at nothing – it's a built-in dummy 'them'. Several Greek idioms carry this silent τα.
ας τα βρούμε (as ta vroume) = literally 'let's find them' = let's make up. The τα (ta) refers to nothing specific – another idiom built on a dummy 'them'.
φοβήθηκα (fovithika) looks passive but just means 'I got scared'. Feeling verbs take this -θηκα past: λυπήθηκα (lipithika) = I felt sad.
English is interested IN something – Greek uses 'for': ενδιαφέρομαι για (endiaferome gia) = I care about. The για (gia) is fixed with this verb.
χαιρόμουν (cheromoun) is the ongoing past: I was glad, again and again. It pairs naturally with κάθε φορά (kathe fora) = every time – repetition takes this tense.
The verb agrees with the thing liked: το ρεμπέτικο (to rebetiko) is one thing, so μου αρέσει (mou aresi) stays singular – 'it pleases me'.
Liking many things makes the verb plural: τα τραγούδια (ta tragoudia) are plural, so it's μου αρέσουν (mou aresoun) – 'they please me'.
ανεβάζω (anevazo) means 'raise' – online it means release: ανεβάζει νέο τραγούδι (anevazi neo tragoudi) = drops a new song. New music gets 'raised' onto the internet.
θερινό σινεμά (therino sinema) = the open-air summer cinema – outdoor screenings are a beloved Greek summer ritual, not a novelty.
